passage: So, you want the story I'm least proud of? Fine. I'm Damini, and in Class 10 my closest friend was Lalremsiami. Some girls in our section started giggling and copying her accent every time she answered in class. One evening she messaged me, "I don't want to go tomorrow." And I typed back, "Yaar, you're too sensitive. Just toughen up, ignore them." I remember feeling almost relieved after I sent it, like the problem was now hers to fix, not mine. She replied with one word: "ok." Next day she sat with her head down all through English. Honestly? Watching them tease her made my stomach twist, and telling her to be stronger was easier than standing next to her. It took me a month to say sorry.

qa.q: What did Damini type back when Lalremsiami said she didn't want to go tomorrow?
qa.a: Damini typed, "Yaar, you're too sensitive. Just toughen up, ignore them."

qa.q: Why did Damini feel almost relieved after sending that message?
qa.a: Telling Lalremsiami to toughen up made the problem hers to fix, so Damini no longer had to face the stomach-twisting discomfort of standing up to the girls.

qa.q: At which point could Damini have chosen differently, and what could that look like?
qa.a: When the "I don't want to go tomorrow" message came, Damini could have asked what was happening, offered to sit with her, and suggested telling a teacher together.

qa.q: What might the one-word reply "ok" tell us about Lalremsiami?
qa.a: It may show Lalremsiami felt shut down and alone, as if even her closest friend thought the teasing was her own fault 🥺.

grounding: A teenager looking back admits telling a bullied friend to toughen up because that was easier than facing the discomfort of standing by the friend.

passage: Farhan here; I'm in the same volleyball batch as Mehak and Sonali. Last week, after practice, two senior players kept flicking Sonali's ponytail and calling her "crybaby" because she had missed a serve and teared up. Sonali's face went blotchy. Mehak was standing right there with me. She laughed a little, then said, "Sonali, stop being so touchy. Seniors joke. Toughen up." Sonali just nodded and went to refill her bottle, alone. I can't say what Mehak was thinking. She kept tugging at her wristband and didn't look at the seniors once. On the bus home she sat with Sonali but talked only about the match.

qa.q: What were the two senior players calling Sonali?
qa.a: They were calling her "crybaby" and flicking her ponytail after she missed a serve and teared up.

qa.q: What might Mehak's tugging at her wristband suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It may suggest Mehak felt uneasy and wanted to avoid a clash with the seniors, so telling Sonali to toughen up felt like the safer option.

qa.q: What choice could Mehak have made at the moment the seniors started teasing?
qa.a: Mehak could have stood beside Sonali, said "That's not funny," and later told the coach what the seniors were doing.

qa.q: If you were Sonali, what would you want from Mehak on the bus home?
qa.a: I would want Mehak to say the teasing was wrong and ask how I was, not just talk about the match.

grounding: A teammate watches a girl tell her teased friend to stop being touchy, placing the problem on the target instead of the seniors.

passage:
Monday: In the class group chat, someone posted a photo of Sarika's lunch with "smelly dabba again lol." Sarika wrote, "why do you always do this." Lavanya messaged her privately: "Chill, you take everything too seriously. Just toughen up." Then she muted the group.
Wednesday: Sarika ate lunch alone in the library corner. Lavanya saw her there and walked past quickly, telling herself Sarika should learn to laugh things off. Her own tiffin tasted like nothing.
The next Monday: Another photo appeared. This time Lavanya took a screenshot, sat down beside Sarika and said, "I was wrong last week. They're the ones doing it. Want to show Miss Roy together?" Sarika hesitated, then nodded. Miss Roy read the chat that same afternoon, thanked them both, and told them she would speak to the class and inform the parents before the day was over.

qa.q: What did Lavanya message Sarika privately on the first Monday?
qa.a: "Chill, you take everything too seriously. Just toughen up."

qa.q: What was Lavanya telling herself on Wednesday, and why might it have felt easier?
qa.a: She told herself Sarika should learn to laugh things off; making Sarika responsible spared Lavanya the awkwardness of facing the class.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Lavanya, and what did she choose to do?
qa.a: When another photo appeared the next Monday, she took a screenshot, sat beside Sarika, owned her mistake and offered to show Miss Roy together.

qa.q: How might the week have felt different for Sarika if Lavanya had sat with Sarika that first Monday?
qa.a: Sarika might not have eaten alone in the library, knowing at least one person saw the teasing as the others' fault, not Sarika's.

grounding: Over a week, a girl first tells her mocked classmate to toughen up to avoid discomfort, then shifts responsibility back to the bullies.

passage:
Mitul, you told your friend to stop being such a baby about the boys teasing him. I said the same thing once, at fifteen, and I've never forgotten it.
At my school in Nagpur, the older girls called my friend Sushmita 'Moti' every day at the water cooler and made pig noises. She came to me with red eyes. And I, Irawati, her best friend, said, 'Arre, you're too touchy. Toughen up and ignore them.'
It was easier for me. If the trouble was her softness, then I didn't have to face those girls.
Sushmita stopped telling me things after that. All that summer she went to the water cooler alone, or not at all.
Years later she said, 'I didn't need to be tougher. I needed you next to me.'
So, Mitul. Tomorrow, stand next to him.

qa.q: What did the older girls call Sushmita at the water cooler?
qa.a: They called her 'Moti' and made pig noises.

qa.q: Why did telling Sushmita to toughen up feel easier to young Irawati?
qa.a: If the problem was Sushmita's softness, Irawati did not have to face the older girls; blaming Sushmita's sensitivity let Irawati dodge a frightening confrontation.

qa.q: What choice does Irawati hope Mitul will make tomorrow, and why?
qa.a: To stand next to the friend being teased; Sushmita's words show that a bullied person needs company, not advice to be tougher.

qa.q: What was that summer like for Sushmita after Irawati's reply?
qa.a: Sushmita stopped confiding and went to the cooler alone or not at all, left to face the teasing without the friend she had counted on.

grounding: An elder recalls telling a bullied friend to toughen up, which spared the observer discomfort by making the target responsible.

subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]
passage:
The school bus was stuck in the flooded underpass, windows fogged, forty kids shouting over the rain. At the back, two Class 12 boys were replaying Uma's dance clip from Annual Day on a phone, adding snorting sounds each time she spun.
Uma, three seats ahead, turned round to Pankaj. 'Tell them to stop. Please.'
Pankaj looked at the Class 12 boys, then at the water rising outside. 'Uma, you're too sensitive, yaar. They're seniors. Just toughen up and ignore it.'
She faced the front again, shoulders up near her ears.
The bus crawled out of the underpass forty minutes late. At her stop Uma got off without saying bye. Pankaj watched her walk fast through the puddles, and for the rest of the ride he couldn't look toward the back seats.

qa.q: What were the Class 12 boys replaying on the phone?
qa.a: Uma's dance clip from Annual Day, with snorting sounds added each time she spun.

qa.q: Why did telling Uma to toughen up feel like the easier option to Pankaj?
qa.a: The boys were seniors and the bus was stuck; speaking up felt risky, so making Uma's sensitivity the problem let Pankaj avoid that discomfort.

qa.q: What could Pankaj have chosen instead when Uma asked for help?
qa.a: He could have moved next to her, told the seniors to put the phone away, or helped her report it to a teacher later; backing her up is what she asked for.

qa.q: How might Uma feel about Pankaj after that bus ride?
qa.a: Uma likely feels let down and alone, since the friend she turned to made her the problem; leaving without saying bye suggests she is hurt.

grounding: A teenager asked for help while a friend is mocked tells her she is too sensitive, shifting the problem onto the target to avoid his own discomfort.
